disagreements.topic: Is Google TPU meaningfully cheaper than NVIDIA GPUs for inference?

positions.claim: TPU v6e (Trillium) delivers roughly 4x better price-performance than H100 for LLM training, recommendation systems, and batch inference, at ~$0.39/chip-hour committed-use.

That '4x' figure traces to unsourced or misattributed claims (a nonexistent MLPerf v4.1 LLM submission); Artificial Analysis' own measured data shows TPU v6e is only roughly competitive with H100 in offline/peak-throughput batch serving ($0.62 vs $0.67-0.69 per million tokens) and about 5x more expensive than H100 in interactive serving ($5.13 vs $1.06 per million tokens at 30 tok/s/user).

disagreements.topic: Does AMD MI300X/MI325X beat NVIDIA H100/H200 for LLM inference?

positions.claim: MI300X/MI325X win on performance-per-dollar and absolute throughput for large dense models (Llama3 405B), high concurrency/large-batch serving, and workloads tolerant of higher per-token latency, due to larger HBM capacity (192-256GB vs 80-141GB) letting more of a large model fit without extra parallelism.

H100/H200 win decisively on latency-sensitive, low-concurrency interactive serving and on raw measured GEMM throughput (14-22% higher achieved BF16/FP8 FLOP/s than MI300X in independent benchmarks), reflecting NVIDIA's more mature TRT-LLM/vLLM kernel optimization on Hopper.

disagreements.topic: Do vendor-submitted MLPerf numbers represent real-world serving performance?

positions.claim: NVIDIA's own MLPerf Inference v5.0 submissions show GB200 NVL72 at up to 3.4x per-GPU and 30x system-level throughput over 8x H200, using NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM stack tuned specifically for the benchmark.

Independent, continuously-run benchmarks using off-the-shelf open-source serving stacks (vLLM, SGLang) show materially smaller and more workload-dependent gaps between Blackwell and Hopper, and note that 'open source vLLM for Hopper is faster than mostly open source TRT-LLM' in some configurations — i.e., MLPerf's framework-optimized numbers are a ceiling, not a typical-deployment number.

disagreements.topic: What does NVIDIA's '30x inference speedup' for GB200 NVL72 actually measure?

positions.claim: GB200 NVL72 delivers 30x higher LLM inference throughput than the same GPU count of H100, framed as a single headline multiplier.

The underlying per-GPU numbers (150 vs. 3.4 tokens/sec/GPU on GPT-MoE-1.8T, a ~44x per-GPU ratio) and NVIDIA's own MLPerf-submitted per-GPU figures (3.1-3.4x on Llama workloads) show the 30x is a system-level composite of per-GPU gains times having 9x more GPUs in an NVL72 rack than a comparable H100 InfiniBand cluster — not a like-for-like per-chip speedup, and the specific multiplier is workload- and configuration-dependent (GPT-MoE-1.8T vs. Llama 3.1 405B vs. Llama 2 70B give different ratios in NVIDIA's own materials).

disagreements.topic: Whose next-gen flagship wins on paper: NVIDIA Rubin or AMD MI455X?

positions.claim: AMD's own published comparison shows MI455X ahead of NVIDIA Vera Rubin on every listed metric: 40 vs. 35 PFLOPS FP4 (+15%), 20 vs. 18 PFLOPS FP8/FP6, 5 vs. 4 PFLOPS FP16/BF16, 432GB vs. 288GB memory (+50%), 23.3 vs. 22.0 TB/s bandwidth (+6%).

NVIDIA's own materials for Rubin state a different, non-directly-comparable headline figure — 50 petaflops of NVFP4 for 'AI inference' — which is higher than the 35 PFLOPS AMD's chart attributes to Rubin, and NVIDIA's pages do not state an HBM4 bandwidth figure at all; the 35 PFLOPS/22.0TB/s numbers in the AMD comparison chart are AMD's own characterization of a competitor's part, not confirmed by NVIDIA, and the basis (dense vs. sparse, training vs. inference peak) is unstated on both sides, so neither the AMD comparison nor a naive reading of NVIDIA's 50 PFLOPS figure should be taken as an apples-to-apples spec-sheet comparison.

disagreements.topic: Is Google TPU actually cheap at the $0.39/chip-hour Introl claimed?

positions.claim: TPU v6e (Trillium) committed-use pricing is ~$0.39/chip-hour, underpinning a '4x better price-performance than H100' claim.

Google's own live TPU pricing page shows Trillium's cheapest listed rate — the 3-year commitment — at $1.22/chip-hour, more than 3x the Introl figure, and on-demand is $2.70/chip-hour; no listed rate anywhere on Google's own pricing table is close to $0.39. This directly corroborates S28's independent conclusion that the Introl '4x cheaper' claim is unsourced/wrong.
